projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Kenneth Badke was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Could you please tell us, Mr. Badke, what kind of civilian work you did before entering the Army?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I've always worked for myself.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Any kind -- what kind of work were you doing?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Before I entered the Army?

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Right. What kind of work were you doing for yourself?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I worked at a Y camp handling horses, teaching children to ride, and I don't come from a horse family.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, you developed that on your own then?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: That's something I developed on my own, my love for horses. I always -- but came from -- you, you made one mistake. I'm not -- I was not born in Georgia.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh. No --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Did you say that?

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I meant to say the year that you were born. But you said your place of birth was Cleveland, Ohio?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Yeah, east of Cleveland. It was in the country --

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: -- east --

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: In the country? Okay.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Yeah, in the country.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Did that help with your interest in horses then?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Oh, yes. I came from horse country.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Polo was the big game.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Yeah. I came from Mayfield Heights in Gates Mills, Ohio. That's east -- that's part of Cleveland in a sense. And I just -- horses were the big business of my dad, being a YMCA executive, we had a Y camp, YMCA camp, and that's where I fell in love with the horses.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I had to, I had to shovel manure when I was a kid.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: That was part of it, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: That was part of it, yeah.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Well, did you have siblings who had that kind of interest also?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: No, just me.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Okay. You were the only child then?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: No. I had, I had three brothers.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see. But they were not interested and didn't have the same interests --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: No. They were in different directions.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: We all went in different directions.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: My oldest brother was, he was a college man, and he completed his college, and he was an engineer. I was always involved with the things that nature produces, and my younger brother was -- my younger brother was an engineer, and my youngest brother is -- was a doctor, became a doctor.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: So we had --

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Different interests?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: -- different interests.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Definitely different interests.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Definitely.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: What age were you when you entered the Army?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Let's see. I was -- in '22. I think I was 30 -- 29.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: 29. Did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: No. I was drafted.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Drafted, okay.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Drafted.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Drafted.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Could you tell us something about that, about entering and your training to start with?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Well, went to -- this is odd, this is the oddest thing in the world. You never count on the Army giving you an assignment that is to your benefit. Loved horses. Ohio State University, went to Ohio State University and was involved with the ROTC program at Ohio State. When you enlisted at Ohio State and you were healthy, you had ROTC.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: And the ROTC at Ohio State was horse-drawn artillery.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, my goodness.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: So, when I was drafted out of Ohio State University, I said, "Oh, boy, artillery, horse-drawn artillery." I wound up in the Medical Department in the Army, and I was a medic from the time I got drafted 'til the time I retired. I was involved with the Medical Department in the Army.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Where did you go for training when you were first drafted?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Camp Joseph T. Robinson, Little Rock, Arkansas.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: And what kinds of things did you have to do there?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: That was Medical Department training. It was -- that was -- all of the people that went into the Medical Department in the Army trained at Joseph.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Well, they took their basic training there. From the basic training, I went to, oh, let's see, Camp (Adare), Oregon, in the Medical Department to -- we were getting two divisions ready to go over to the Far East, and from the Medical Company at Camp Joseph T. Robinson, I applied for ROTC. I applied for training to become an officer, so they sent me to Texas.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: And I graduated from Camp Barkeley, Texas, and was a Second Lieutenant in the Medical Service Corps.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: And what age were you by that time?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Getting close to 30.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: And let's see. We went to -- my first assignment, odd as it may seem, my first assignment, which I didn't apply for, but they sent me back to my hometown at Cleveland, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, my goodness.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: And I was at Krile General Hospital in Cleveland. And from there, I went -- I got an assignment to the Far East and got out to Fort Lewis, Washington. And when I got to Fort Lewis, Washington, they reassigned me to France. So I came all the way back across the country, and my wife joined me and I went to France.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see. And so you had married --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Well, I was married in 1944.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see. Did you all have --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I was married before I was in the Army.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see. Did you all have any children at that time?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Not at that time.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Right. So she went to France with you then?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: No. She got to the East Coast --

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, to the East Coast?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: -- and said, "No, you can't go to France." She went, she went back to Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: And in fact, our first child was born, I'm in Germany, she's in the U.S.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, good.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: And she came over -- it's odd. She came overseas with the first load of dependents that were assigned to -- that came into Germany.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, that's really interesting. And did you all have quarters already set up for families --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Yeah, they did.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: -- at that time?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: They did. Yes, they did. We had a house in Stuttgart which was -- I was assigned to the hospital at Stuttgart, in the Army Hospital in Stuttgart, and lived in a house right above the hospital. We had a whole section of Stuttgart. That was back -- I used to -- I like to say to people that was back when we owned Germany.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see. Oh, goodness. Well, where did you go after that?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I stayed in, I stayed in Germany until 1949, and then I came to -- I got orders to go to Augusta, Georgia, and the adjunct of the hospital, when he called me in and said, "Ken, you've got orders," he told me, "You have orders to go to Fort" -- it was Camp Gordon, Georgia. And I said, "Where in the devil is Camp Gordon, Georgia?" He said, "That's Augusta." I said, "I never heard of Augusta. Where is Augusta?" He gets the map out, and he says, "Right there." I came to Augusta, been here ever since.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, been here since. Okay.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: All right. Well, what about the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I spent exactly -- let's see. I got here in March of '49, and I went to Korea. The war in Korea started June the 25th of '50, and July the 18th I was in Korea, of 1950. So we, we almost didn't get to land the boat.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Because the North Koreans were almost into Pusan. They had taken over everything. We had to fight our way out of Pusan.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Well, can you tell more about what went on there in the Korean War for you, your experiences there?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. We -- I was the, I was the Field First Sergeant of the Medical Company of the Ninth Regimen of the Second Division. And we got to Korea in a hurry. Went to Fort Lewis, Washington. Here again, I'm back out in Washington. Went to Fort Lewis, joined the Ninth Regimen of the Second Division, packed my bags, and got on a boat. We landed in Korea on the 18th day of July. We were in a hurry.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Yes, you were.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: And fought our way out of Pusan to the Nakdong River, and we were there -- we were stopped at the Nakdong River. And it's odd, on my birthday, we crossed the Nakdong River and headed north. I laugh because I've got friends that have said, "Well, what did you all do in Korea? Did you have a good time over there?" And I said, "We didn't have time to have a good time." We went right past Seoul. We went to the North Korea, fought to the North Korean capitol, and all the way to the Yalu River. I have stuck my foot in the Yalu River at that time. We were -- we got into -- when we left the North -- before we left the North Korean capitol, we were told that we should not disturb the Chinese, don't bother the Chinese, they are in North Korea to guard the reservoirs. Biggest mistake General MacArthur ever made. We went past the -- the Chinese let us go right on in. We never got out. The Chinese were behind us. The Chinese were there not to protect the reservoirs. Who wants to protect a body of water that's stuck up in the mountains? So that was -- we couldn't get out, the Medical Company. None of us could get out. We had 100,000 Chinese behind us.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: My goodness.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I, on the 27th day of November, 1950, the Medical Company was off into a valley, small valley on the road out of, out of -- I can't think of the, the road back into Kunari, and my driver woke me up and he said, "Hey Sarge," he said, "We got military people going by us." Walked over to -- this is odd. Walked over to the side of the hill and looked down on the road that wound around the mountains there, and Chinese troops were going by all night long, six abreast and double-time. And there was no way to get out of there, no way. We were -- in fact, they went by us. They knew we were there. They kept coming by us, and on the 1st day of December of 1950, they stopped. They all got by us. That's when the 100,000 of them went by, and they stopped and picked us up.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: And where did they take you?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: We went to a mining camp. They took us to a mining camp and put us in the mines. Any prisoners that they captured they took and they put in these mines in these mining camps. They kept us there for about two weeks in those mines.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Did they harm anyone before you got there, or did they just take everybody captive?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: No. They just -- whoever they took captive they put in the mines. And you got a hole in the wall about as big as this room and two people standing there guarding it, they didn't have to worry about a lot of troops. And that's where things got worse. We had no food.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: For the entire two weeks --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: We had very little water. You couldn't go out of the mines, and they had kept their horses and their mules in those mines. It was quite a, it was quite an experience really.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I'm sure that it was.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: But that's when they took us out of the mines. They took us to another mining camp in -- it was north of there. And I can remember when they took us out of that mining camp, I can remember Christmas Eve of 1950, they marched us over the tallest mountain in Korea. It was a full moon that night, just a huge full moon that night, and we marched over that and we marched -- we sweated going up the mountain, and we froze to death coming down the mountain. And they marched us there, I think, until December -- I mean January, January the 15th, and that's when we arrived at what was Camp Five. It was a town on the Yalu River in North Korea. And I stayed there until -- at that camp, and we tried to organize the camp, and the Chinese didn't like that real well, so they took all of the sergeants, brought boats up the river. That was in June of 1951. They brought boats up the river and put all the sergeants, whether they were British, Turkish, or American or French, they took all the sergeants and put them on boats and took us up the Yalu River to a camp at the apex of North Korea and run everybody else out of town. Put us in that town, and we stayed there until I was released on my wedding anniversary.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: And when was that?

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, so that was for a long time?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Yes. And what's your anniversary date?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: My anniversary then was the 10th of September.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: 10th of September?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Yeah, 1953.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Well, when you all were in that camp where you had so many different kinds of people, did they feed you then?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Oh, yes. They decided they better -- the peace negotiations started.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: When the peace negotiations started, the United States showed up with a list of all the prisoners that they had. Of course, they fed their prisoners. They kept them alive. There was medical and so forth, so on, according to the Geneva Convention which the Chinese didn't believe in. So the Chinese, when they showed up, they had made such publicity out of the number of people that they had captured that Uncle Sam said, "Hey, where's the rest of them?" And they had to say, "Well, they died." And they lost face.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: How many did they say had passed away?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Well, we know. 2,800.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: 2,800 people. There was a difference between the regimen, and Uncle Sam said, "Well, what happened to them?" And it was a very losing face as far as the Chinese were concerned, the Koreans. So they decided they'd better feed us and keep what was left alive, which they did.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: And how many were left?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I can't --

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Approximately?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Approximately, there might have been -- I think there were 1,800-some like that.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: 18. So more than half had passed away by that time?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Was it from starvation or the conditions or --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Both.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Both. We used to stack the dead up, couldn't bury them. We'd go -- they'd have burial details, and we'd take the bodies up under the hillsides and scrape the snow and the stones away and lay them on the ground and then cover them with snow and stones. You couldn't dig a hole.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Because the ground was just frozen?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I've seen the Yalu River covered with ice 12 feet thick. You could have landed an airplane on that Yalu River, which is just absolutely amazing. It would get cold, get 50, 60 degrees below zero.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Did they keep you all warm during that time?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Sometimes. We had -- like I said, the peace negotiations just changed, the whole thing just rolled over. They brought us food. Instead of -- rice was a delicacy. We ate millet and soybeans. Now, you try a diet of millet and soybeans for six months, and you see what happens. Just absolutely would tear you up, millet and soybeans.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: So then, when you started getting rice, that was much better --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Well, yeah. Your diet changed a little bit, and then they started -- they would -- they brought in some goats. We ate goat meat, and they allowed us to fish in the Yalu River; so, being a big fisherman, I made fishing line out of my socks.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I unraveled my socks and made fishing line out of it, and I bribed the kids that were in the town where we were, I bribed those kids to give me some fishing hooks.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, my goodness. Well, you were resourceful, no doubt about that.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: You had to be resourceful. Yep. And in order to -- we -- anything, anything that popped its head up through the snow and was green and was growing went into a can, and you boiled it and ate it. But that's all one thing I've never been afraid of. I've never been afraid to eat anything.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I guess not after that experience.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: No, not afraid to eat anything, at least I'll try it.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Well, during World War II, what assignments did you have?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: World War II, after I graduated, I got assigned to the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Was the hospital, 62nd Field Hospital, we were assigned to the Air Force, Istres Air Base in Southern France. When the invasion in Southern France, we went in after that and was assigned to the field hospital there. And we stayed in Southern France until the war ended, and we went into Germany.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Okay. Then that's when your family was eventually able to join you?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Eventually.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: In Germany then.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: So, when you all were in Germany, what was some of the experiences that you had as a family?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I had a good time.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Well, good.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I had a good time, good time in Germany.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: And how many children did you end up having?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I've got, let's see, Kenny, there's Michael, there's Jeff. Kenny, Michael, Jeff, three boys.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: That's great. That's great. Were they all there with you in Germany? Were they all --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Oh, no, no, no, no.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: My first son was born before -- came over with my wife.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Right. Yes.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: And he was just a little biddy shaver.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Learned to speak German.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, but the others weren't born until you got back?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: They were all born after we got back.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Where did you live when you got back?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Augusta, Georgia.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Augusta, Georgia. That's right. You said you've been here ever since, didn't you?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Augusta, Georgia.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: All right. So your children grew up going to schools in Augusta?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: In Augusta. Yep, they all got educated in Augusta, still live in Augusta.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: They all live in Augusta.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Right. Well, that's good. You're able to see them then?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Yeah. Well, my oldest son, he kicked around for a while, but he came back to Augusta. He retired.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: All of my kids are retired.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, well that's great then. That's nice.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Including me.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Well, when you got back to Augusta and got out of the military, I know you said you've always worked for yourself, but what kind of things did you do at that point?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Well, I was a salesman.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: First got out, I had a friend of mine who owned the Pontiac dealership here in town, an old German, and two old German boys, Walter and Willie. And they took care of my wife all the time I was kicking around the world, and they always kept her cars and everybody would ____+. When I got out, they were waiting for me. They said, "We have a job for you."

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I sold Pontiacs for about, good Lord, ten years, I guess.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Then I decided it was time for me, it was time for me to go out on my own and be a salesman. So I went into the real estate business.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, real estate. I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Been in it ever since.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, all right. And you're doing some developing now, you said?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I live -- I live in the development that I first helped develop. I was with a group called Goshen Developers.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see. So you were in with a group developing Goshen Plantation to begin with?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Uh-huh. I'm still there. They're gone, but I'm still there. We're developing land. In fact, the one development we're going to put in, which is a gated community in Goshen, it's called the Village at Goshen. And then we have another 150 acres right across the street from there that we're going to develop.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Goshen, originally Goshen went -- Goshen Plantation was a plantation back during the -- after the -- Lord, that goes way back to the 1800s.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: And it's still called Goshen. It's goshen -- when people go into the South Richmond County, that's Goshen.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: That's the Goshen area. I see.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: When you hit Tobacco Road and go south, that's Goshen. That all is Goshen.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Is there anything else you would want to tell us about, about your life, anything about the war, your experiences or what you're doing now in terms of veterans activities or what you have done?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Well, veterans activities, I'm a member of the POW group here in Augusta. That's basically what I've been involved with.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: But after I, after I hit that 80th birthday, my wife said, "You are retired." And so I came down here. I said, "I need a job."

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Oh, so you volunteered --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I volunteered.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: -- at the hospital then?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Yeah, I volunteered at the hospital. And I've got everything else going on, so I just -- I stay busy.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: You do. You have a full life it sounds like?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Yeah. I stay busy, sleep late but stay busy.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: That's great. You've earned all that, haven't you?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: Yes, ma'am.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Well, I certainly appreciate your interview today. I'm Jo Dye, and I'm a volunteer with the AARP, with the Veterans History Project, and we thank you so much that you were willing to share with us and to have your information recorded with the Library of Congress.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Badke
sp.p: I certainly appreciate it.

sp.speaker: Josephine Dye
sp.p: Okay. (Interview concluded.)
